newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Labour disputes hit South Korea industrial output.
newsitem.headline: Labour disputes hit South Korea industrial output.

text.p: Labour unrest hampered South Korea's industrial output in January, but a slowdown in consumer spending kept inflation in check, government ministries said on Friday.
"Industrial production was badly damaged by almost a month of strikes," said an official at the National Statistical Office (NSO).
"But consumer inflation was stabilised by a business slowdown, which forced consumers to cut back on spending," a Finance Ministry official said.
The NSO figures showed industrial output in January rose 5.9 percent year-on-year, sharply down from a 12.4 percent gain a year earlier.
Vehicle output, which was hit hardest by the work stoppages, dropped 34.1 percent on the year, while garments and fur products fell 22.3 percent, the NSO figures showed.
Nationwide wildcat strikes erupted late in December to protest the forced passage of a new labour law that allows companies to lay off workers and replace strikers.
Ex-factory shipment rose only 2.6 percent in line with the slower production, compared with a 13.6 percent rise a year earlier, they said.
Factories operated at 77 percent of their capacity in January, down from 82 percent a year before.
With the sagging production, investment also slumped as companies froze plans to buy capital goods.
Machinery orders in the domestic market in January fell 27.5 percent year-on-year, compared with a 34.3 percent rise a year ago, the NSO figures showed.
Machinery imports declined 16.2 percent year-on-year, against a 45.1 percent rise.
The Finance Ministry said the consumer price index (CPI), South Korea's leading inflation indicator, rose 4.9 percent in February on the year, down from a 5.1 percent rise a year earlier.
In January, the CPI increased 4.7 percent compared with a 5.1 percent rise a year before.
The ministry said overall prices for industrial products rose by a relatively low 5.2 percent on the year, helped by a decline in the prices of computers and television sets.
"Basically, consumers are delaying their spending plans, expecting a further slowdown in the economy," said the ministry official.
The NSO figures showed wholesale and retail sales rose a mere 1.4 percent in January, down from a 4.5 percent rise a year ago.
Personal computer prices fell 24.5 percent in February and television prices lost 6.2 percent, the ministry said.
Prices of agricultural, livestock and fishery products rose 3.7 percent on the year and public service charges rose 5.0 percent, it said.

The NSO figures showed output of heavy industrial goods rose 8.6 percent year-on-year in January against a 15.2 percent rise a year ago, while light industrial products fell 5.4 percent, against a rise of 2.7 percent.
Ex-factory shipments for export in the month increased 10 percent year-on-year, against a 24 percent rise the year before.
Shipments to the domestic market fell 0.3 percent, compared with a rise of 9.9 percent a year ago, the NSO figures showed.
